blocks.html: Picture a hot, dry desert that stretches farther than you can see. Now picture a river running through the middle of it, with a long green ribbon of fields on each bank. That ribbon was ancient Egypt. Almost everyone lived on it, close to the water.
Egypt was a long, narrow green strip along the Nile River, with dry desert on both sides. Without the Nile, there would have been no Egypt.

It almost never rains in Egypt. The river brought the water that people, animals and crops needed. Where the water reached, plants grew; where it did not, the land stayed sand and rock. The Egyptians even named the two kinds of land: Kemet, "the black land," for the dark soil by the river, and Deshret, "the red land," for the desert.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The Nile runs up the middle of Egypt. Tap a dot to see what was there. Every big site sits close to the river.

blocks.title: Where would you build a village?
blocks.q: You are an Egyptian farmer 4,000 years ago. Where is the best place for your village: deep in the desert, or near the Nile?
steps: Think about what a village needs: water to drink and water for crops.
In the desert there is almost no rain and no river.
Beside the Nile there is water and rich soil.
blocks.a: Near the Nile, on the green strip of farmland.

blocks.html: Many people picture Egypt as all sand, or as a jungle. It was neither. Look at the map: the sites line up along the river like beads on a string. People lived on the thin green ribbon, with desert all around it.
A Greek visitor, Herodotus, called Egypt "the gift of the river." He meant that the land itself, its soil and its farms, came from the Nile. You can explore every site on the big map of Egypt.
You know that Egypt was a green strip along the Nile. But which way does the water go? On most maps north is at the top, and the Nile surprises people: it flows up the map.
The Nile flows from south to north. It starts deep in Africa and empties into the Mediterranean Sea. Near the sea it splits into branches that fan out in a triangle called the Delta.

Water always runs downhill. The land far to the south, in the mountains of East Africa, is high. The Mediterranean coast is low. So the river runs north, from high ground to the sea. The Delta got its name from the Greek letter delta, Δ, because the branches spread out in a triangle.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Follow the Nile from Khartoum, where two rivers meet, all the way north to the Delta and the sea.

blocks.title: Which way to float?
blocks.q: A boat floats on the Nile with no sail and no rowing, from Karnak toward Giza. Will it get there?
steps: The current flows south to north.
Giza is north of Karnak.
So the current carries the boat toward Giza.
blocks.a: Yes. Giza is downstream (north) of Karnak.

blocks.html: Thinking rivers must flow "down" the map, toward the south. Rivers flow downhill, not down the page. Check a map: the Nile's mouths are at the top, on the Mediterranean, so it flows north.
The Nile is one of the two longest rivers in the world. Its two main branches, the White Nile and the Blue Nile, meet at Khartoum in Sudan and flow north together into Egypt.
Since the Nile flows north, people in Egypt talked about going "up the river" (south) and "down the river" (north). That gave the two halves of the country their names.
Upper Egypt is the south: the long, narrow valley, up the river. Lower Egypt is the north: the wide, flat Delta near the sea, down the river.

The names come from the river, not from the map. Upper Egypt is upstream, closer to where the Nile comes from. Lower Egypt is downstream, where the river ends. On a map with north at the top, that puts "Upper" at the bottom!

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Find the words LOWER EGYPT near the Delta and UPPER EGYPT down the valley.

blocks.title: Which half?
blocks.q: Karnak is far to the south, in the narrow river valley. Is it in Upper or Lower Egypt?
steps: South means up the river.
Up the river is Upper Egypt.
blocks.a: Upper Egypt.

blocks.html: Thinking "Upper" means the top of the map. Remember: Upper = upstream = south. Ask "Is it up the river or down the river?" and the name follows.
The Nile did something amazing every year: it rose, spilled over its banks and covered the fields with water. Egyptians did not fear this flood. They waited for it and hoped it would be just right.
Every summer the Nile rose and flooded the valley. When the water went down, it left a layer of rich, dark mud (silt) that made the fields fertile for the next crop.

The flood began far away. Each summer, heavy rains fell on the mountains of Ethiopia, far to the south. That water rushed down into the Nile, which swelled and flowed north into Egypt. The muddy water carried soil from those mountains and left it on Egypt's fields, like a fresh layer of plant food every year.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The flood water came from the south. The town of Elephantine, at the First Cataract, was among the first to see it rise.

blocks.title: A low flood
blocks.q: One year the Nile rises only a little. What happens to the farms?
steps: The water does not reach many fields.
Those fields get no new mud and stay dry.
Fewer crops grow, so there is less food.
blocks.a: A poor harvest, and people may go hungry.

blocks.title: A huge flood
blocks.q: Another year the Nile rises much higher than usual. Is that good news?
steps: A little extra water is fine.
But a very high flood can wash away houses and canals.
blocks.a: No: too much water can be as bad as too little.

blocks.html: Thinking the flood was a disaster. For Egyptians it was the most important event of the year: a good flood meant a good harvest. They even measured it with marked steps called nilometers. The flood god Hapi was pictured as a plump, well-fed man.
Today the Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970, holds the water back, so the Nile no longer floods each year.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Nile" (the flood and the Aswan High Dam)

blocks.html: You have seen how the yearly flood shaped life in Egypt. It even shaped the calendar. Egyptians did not count four seasons like spring, summer, fall and winter. They counted three, and all three were about the river and the fields.
The Egyptian year had three seasons: Akhet, the flood; Peret, the growing time; and Shemu, the harvest. Each season had four months of 30 days.

In Egypt, weather changes little: it is warm and dry most of the year. What changed was the river. First the fields were under water (Akhet). Then the water went down and seeds sprouted in the mud (Peret). Then the crops were cut (Shemu). Naming the seasons after the river told everyone what work came next.

head: Season
What happened
About when
rows: water goes down; planting and growing
blocks.cap: The three seasons in order.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The word for "day," hrw. The last sign, the sun, is a hint sign for words about time.

blocks.title: Counting the days
blocks.q: Each season had 4 months, and each month had 30 days. How many days were in the three seasons?
steps: One season: 4 × 30 = 120 days.
Three seasons: 3 × 120 = 360 days.
Egyptians added 5 extra feast days at the end of the year.
blocks.a: 360 days, and with the 5 extra days, 365.

blocks.html: Expecting four seasons named for the weather. Egypt's three seasons followed the river. A quick check: Akhet comes first because the year started with the flood.
Because the Nile flows north, and Egypt was a long strip beside it, the river was the best road in the land. Stone, grain, animals, people and even the king traveled by boat.
Going north, boats floated with the current. Going south, they raised a sail, because the wind in Egypt usually blows from the north.

Two natural forces worked together. The current always runs north. The usual wind blows from the north toward the south. So a boat could ride the current one way and the wind the other way. On the trip north, sailors took the sail down and steered, or rowed to go faster.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Trips between Memphis in the north and Elephantine in the south were one long boat ride.

blocks.title: From Karnak to Memphis
blocks.q: A boat carries grain from Karnak to Memphis. Memphis is to the north. What moves the boat?
steps: North is downstream.
The current flows north.
blocks.a: The current. The sail can come down.

blocks.title: From Memphis to Elephantine
blocks.q: Now the boat goes from Memphis to Elephantine, far to the south. What moves it?
steps: South is upstream, against the current.
The wind usually blows from the north toward the south.
A sail catches that wind.
blocks.a: The north wind, filling the sail.

blocks.html: Thinking boats needed their sails both ways. Going north, the current did the work. Egyptians even wrote "travel north" with a picture of a boat with no sail, and "travel south" with a boat with its sail up.

Small boats were made of bundles of papyrus reeds. Big ones were built of wood, often cedar brought from Lebanon. A full-size wooden boat of King Khufu, about 43 meters long, was found buried beside the Great Pyramid in 1954.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Great Pyramid of Giza" (the Khufu boat pits)

blocks.html: After the season of the flood, the fields were covered in fresh black mud. Now the farmers got to work. Most Egyptians were farmers, and their crops fed the whole country.

Farmers grew wheat and barley (for bread and beer) and flax (for linen cloth) in the black mud. They dug canals to bring water to the fields and, in later times, lifted water with a shaduf, a bucket on a long pole.

Crops grew only where water reached. The flood soaked the fields once a year, but plants still needed water while they grew. Canals carried river water farther from the banks. The shaduf had a heavy weight on one end of the pole, so lifting a full bucket took little effort.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The wide, flat Delta was Egypt's biggest stretch of farmland.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs

opts.en: a sickle, the tool for cutting grain

blocks.cap: The sickle sign. Real sickles had sharp teeth of flint set in wood.

blocks.title: A farmer's year
blocks.q: Put the farm jobs in order: harvest the grain, wait for the flood to go down, plant the seeds.
steps: First the flood covers the fields (Akhet), so farmers wait for it to go down.
Then they plow and plant in the mud (Peret).
Last they cut the ripe grain (Shemu).
blocks.a: Wait for the flood to go down, plant the seeds, harvest the grain.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians farmed in the sand. Look at the map: farms were only on the green strip the flood reached. One step past it, the desert began.
Oxen pulled wooden plows. At harvest, people cut the grain with sickles, and animals walked over it to knock the grains loose.

sources.name: Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (1927), Sign-list U1 (the sickle)

blocks.html: For about three thousand years, Egypt had a ruler at the top: the king. Today we often call Egypt's kings pharaohs. Where does that word come from? It is older than you might think.
A pharaoh was the king (or, a few times, the queen) of all Egypt. The word comes from the Egyptian per-aa, "Great House," which first meant the royal palace.

People often talk about a leader by naming the building where the leader works, the way news reports say "the White House said…" when they mean the President. Egyptians did the same: "the Great House" came to mean the king who lived in it. That use began in the New Kingdom, more than a thousand years after the first kings.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: per-aa, "Great House": the house plan sign (per) and the column sign (aa, "great").

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: nesu, "king," the word Egyptians used most often.

blocks.title: A title, not a name
blocks.q: Is "Pharaoh" the name of one person?
steps: A name belongs to one person, like Khufu or Ramesses.
"Pharaoh" was used for every king, one after another.
blocks.a: No. It is a title, like "king."

blocks.html: Thinking "Pharaoh" was one person's name. It is a title, and Egyptians mostly said nesu, "king." Every pharaoh also had his or her own names, written in ovals called cartouches; you will learn to read them in Reading a Cartouche.

Egyptians believed the king stood between the people and the gods. The king led the army, ran the country with the help of officials, and made offerings in the temples so that the world stayed in order.

sources.name: Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (1927), Sign-list O1 (house) and O29 (column)

blocks.html: You met the pharaoh and the two halves of Egypt. A king could show which land he ruled just by what he wore on his head.

The tall white crown stood for Upper Egypt (the south). The red crown, with a curl in front, stood for Lower Egypt (the north). The double crown, the two put together, meant the king ruled both. Kings also held a crook and a flail.

Crowns worked like flags: anyone could tell at a glance what a king stood for. When Egypt became one kingdom, kings put the two crowns together, so the double crown said "ruler of the Two Lands." The crook is a shepherd's staff: the king guards his people as a shepherd guards sheep.

head: Crown
Looks like
Stands for
rows: tall and white, shaped like a bowling pin
red, flat on top, with a tall back and a curl
the white crown set inside the red one

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: heqa, "ruler." The first sign is the crook itself, the shepherd's staff kings held.

blocks.title: Which crown?
blocks.q: A carving shows a king wearing a tall white crown. Which land does it stand for?
steps: White crown = Upper Egypt.
Upper Egypt is the south, up the river.
blocks.a: Upper Egypt, the south.

blocks.html: Mixing up the crowns. A memory trick: the white crown is tall and points up, like Upper Egypt. The red one has a curl, like a curling branch of the Delta.
Egypt had a white crown and a red crown because, long ago, there were two lands. Egypt did not start out as one country. It became one.
Around 3000 BC, Upper and Lower Egypt were joined into one kingdom. A carved stone called the Narmer Palette shows King Narmer wearing the white crown on one side and the red crown on the other.

Before the kings, people along the Nile lived in villages and small kingdoms. Over many years, rulers from the south grew stronger and took over more land, all the way to the Delta. A king who ruled the whole river could share out its food and water and keep the peace. Ever since, Egyptians called their country "the Two Lands."

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The first kings came hundreds of years before the pyramids. Tap a period to learn more.

blocks.title: Reading the palette
blocks.q: On one side of the palette, Narmer wears the white crown. On the other, the red crown. What does that tell us?
steps: White crown = Upper Egypt.
Red crown = Lower Egypt.
He is shown as king of both.
blocks.a: Narmer is shown as ruler of both lands.

blocks.title: What came first?
blocks.q: Which came first: the joining of Egypt, or the Great Pyramid?
steps: Egypt became one kingdom around 3000 BC.
The Great Pyramid was built for King Khufu around 2560 BC.
Bigger numbers BC are longer ago.
blocks.a: The joining of Egypt, about 400 years earlier.

blocks.html: Thinking Egypt was always one country. It began as smaller lands that were joined. Experts still discuss just how it happened: the palette may show a real war, or it may be a way of saying "this king rules everything."
Later Egyptians remembered a first king called Menes. Many experts think Menes and Narmer were the same king, but nobody is sure.

sources.name: Ian Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000), for the dates (as given in Wikipedia's "Egyptian chronology")

blocks.html: Most pharaohs were men. But a few women ruled Egypt as king, and the most famous of them is Hatshepsut (say it "hat-SHEP-soot").
Hatshepsut ruled Egypt as king for about 15 years in the New Kingdom (c. 1473–1458 BC). She built a great temple at Deir el-Bahari and sent ships to the faraway land of Punt.

When King Thutmose II died, his son Thutmose III was a small child. Hatshepsut, the king's widow, ruled for the boy at first. After a few years she took the title of king herself, and the two ruled side by side. Statues often show her in a king's kilt and headcloth, even with the king's false beard, because that was how a king was supposed to look.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: Hatshepsut ruled about 200 years before Ramesses the Great.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Her temple at Deir el-Bahari sits under the cliffs on the west bank at Thebes. Tap its dot.

blocks.title: A trip to Punt
blocks.q: Hatshepsut's ships came back from Punt with incense trees. How do we know about the trip?
steps: Hatshepsut had the voyage carved on the walls of her temple.
The carvings show the ships, the people of Punt and the trees being loaded.
blocks.a: From the carvings on her temple at Deir el-Bahari.

blocks.html: Thinking only men could be pharaoh. A few women ruled; Hatshepsut is the most famous. Where exactly Punt was is still debated: probably somewhere along the Red Sea coast of Africa.

sources.name: Ian Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000), for the dates (as given in Wikipedia's "Egyptian chronology")

blocks.html: Some pharaohs ruled for only a year or two. Ramesses II ruled for 66 years! Later Egyptians remembered him as a great king, and today we often call him Ramesses the Great.
Ramesses II ruled in the New Kingdom (c. 1279–1213 BC). He built huge temples, like the two at Abu Simbel, fought the Hittites at Kadesh, and later made a peace treaty with them.

A very long reign gave Ramesses time to build. His name was carved all over Egypt, sometimes even on older monuments. At Abu Simbel, four giant statues of him, each about 20 meters tall, were cut out of a cliff. Many people were born, grew up and grew old while he was king.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: His name in a cartouche: the sun (Ra), then signs for ms and s.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Abu Simbel is far to the south, in Nubia.

blocks.title: Saving a temple
blocks.q: In the 1960s a new dam made a huge lake that would cover Abu Simbel. What did people do?
steps: Engineers cut the temples into more than a thousand blocks.
They moved the blocks to higher ground and put them back together (1964–68).
blocks.a: They moved the whole temple, block by block, to higher ground.

blocks.html: Thinking one pharaoh ruled for all of history. There were hundreds of kings over about three thousand years. Even Ramesses, with 66 years, ruled for only a small part of it.
Ramesses had a very large family: lists on his temples name dozens of sons and daughters.

sources.name: Ian Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000), for the dates (as given in Wikipedia's "Egyptian chronology")

blocks.html: Here is a What Is a Pharaoh? who ruled for only about nine years and died young, yet his name is known all over the world: Tutankhamun.

Tutankhamun became king at about eight or nine years old and died at about eighteen (he ruled c. 1336–1327 BC). His small tomb in the Valley of the Kings was found nearly untouched in 1922, full of treasure.

Robbers broke into almost every royal tomb long ago and took the treasure. Tutankhamun's tomb was small and hidden under later rubble, so most of it survived. That is why he is famous: not for great deeds, but because his tomb shows us what a king took with him. Nobody knows for sure why he died so young.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: Tutankhamun, "living image of Amun." The god's name, Amun, is written first out of honor but read last.

blocks.title: A new name
blocks.q: He was born Tutankhaten, "living image of the Aten." Why did he change it to Tutankhamun?
steps: The king before him had put the sun disk, the Aten, above all other gods.
The boy king brought back the old gods, led by Amun.
His new name honored Amun.
blocks.a: To show he had brought back the worship of the god Amun.

blocks.html: Thinking Tutankhamun was the greatest pharaoh. He was a young king who ruled only a short time. He is famous because his tomb was found nearly complete. You can read how it was found in Finding Tutankhamun's Tomb.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: Tutankhamun came after Akhenaten and before Ramesses II.

sources.name: Ian Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000), for the dates (as given in Wikipedia's "Egyptian chronology")

blocks.html: The last What Is a Pharaoh? of ancient Egypt was a queen: Cleopatra VII. She lived much later than the pyramid builders, and her family was not even Egyptian at first.
Cleopatra VII (69–30 BC) was the last ruler of the Ptolemies, a Greek family that ruled Egypt for about 300 years. After she died in 30 BC, Egypt became part of the Roman Empire.

Alexander the Great, from Macedonia in Greece, conquered Egypt in 332 BC. When he died, his general Ptolemy became king, and Ptolemy's family ruled from the city of Alexandria. Most of them spoke only Greek. Cleopatra was the first of her family known to learn the Egyptian language. She lost a war against Rome, and Rome took over Egypt.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: The name Cleopatra in sound signs. This spelling, from an obelisk at Philae, belongs to an earlier queen Cleopatra of the same family.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: From the Great Pyramid to Cleopatra is a very long way.

blocks.title: Closer to us
blocks.q: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC. Is she closer in time to the pyramid builders, or to us?
steps: From c. 2560 BC to 30 BC: about 2,530 years.
From 30 BC to today: about 2,055 years.
2,055 is less than 2,530.
blocks.a: Closer to us!

blocks.html: Thinking Cleopatra lived when the pyramids were built. She lived more than 2,000 years after the Great Pyramid. To her, the pyramids were already ancient.

sources.name: Ian Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000), for the dates (as given in Wikipedia's "Egyptian chronology")

blocks.html: A What Is a Pharaoh? was the most important person in Egypt, so Egyptians believed his life after death mattered for everyone. In the Old Kingdom, kings were buried under some of the biggest buildings ever made: pyramids.
Pyramids were tombs for kings. They were built to protect the king's body and to help him live forever. Each pyramid had temples beside it, where priests brought offerings.

Egyptians believed a person lived on after death, but the body and the offerings had to be cared for. A mountain of stone kept the burial safe and lasted for all time. Many experts think the shape also had a meaning: it may recall the first mound of land that rose out of the water when the world began, or the slanting rays of the sun.

blocks.name: eg-pyramid
blocks.cap: Inside the Great Pyramid: passages lead to rooms deep inside. The king was buried in the King's Chamber.

blocks.title: Palace or tomb?
blocks.q: A pyramid has a small stone room deep inside, with long narrow passages and no windows. Was it a palace for a living king?
steps: A palace needs rooms for living: bedrooms, halls, kitchens.
A pyramid is solid stone with only a few small rooms for a burial.
blocks.a: No. It was a tomb.

blocks.html: Thinking pyramids were palaces or storehouses. They were royal tombs, with temples beside them. Even so, robbers broke into almost all of them long ago, in spite of hidden passages and huge blocking stones.
Egypt has more than a hundred pyramids. In the New Kingdom, kings gave up pyramids and were buried in hidden tombs cut into the rock instead.
The pyramids did not all look the same. The builders learned by trying, and you can see their experiments in the desert today.

The first pyramid, built for King Djoser, had six big steps. Later, King Sneferu built the Bent Pyramid, whose angle changes partway up, and then the Red Pyramid, the first smooth-sided pyramid to be finished. His son Khufu built the Great Pyramid.

Before Djoser, kings were buried under low, flat tombs of mud brick. Djoser's builder, Imhotep, built in stone and stacked six layers, each smaller than the one below. Next, builders tried filling in the steps to make smooth sides. On the Bent Pyramid they changed to a gentler slope partway up, probably because the steep slope was not safe. They used the gentler slope for the Red Pyramid, and it stood firm.

blocks.name: eg-pyramid
blocks.cap: Djoser's Step Pyramid, Sneferu's Bent and Red Pyramids, and Khufu's Great Pyramid, drawn to the same scale.

blocks.title: Put them in order
blocks.q: Order these from oldest to newest: the Great Pyramid, the Step Pyramid, the Bent Pyramid.
steps: Djoser's Step Pyramid came first (c. 2667–2648 BC).
Sneferu's Bent Pyramid came next.
Khufu, Sneferu's son, built the Great Pyramid after that.
blocks.a: Step Pyramid, Bent Pyramid, Great Pyramid.

blocks.html: Thinking every pyramid looks the same. The builders tried steps, then a bent slope, then smooth sides. Check the shape: steps mean early; a bend means Sneferu was still experimenting.

sources.name: Ian Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000), for the dates (as given in Wikipedia's "Egyptian chronology")

blocks.html: After his father's experiments with smooth sides, King Khufu built the biggest pyramid of all at Giza, near today's Cairo. His son and grandson built beside it.
The three great pyramids of Giza belong to Khufu (the biggest), Khafre and Menkaure (the smallest). The Great Sphinx, a lion with a king's head, lies beside the path to Khafre's pyramid.

Each king wanted a tomb near his family's. Khufu's pyramid was about 147 meters tall when it was new, and it stayed the tallest building in the world for more than 3,700 years. Khafre's looks almost as tall because it stands on higher ground. The Sphinx was carved out of the bedrock itself, about 73 meters long.

blocks.name: eg-pyramid
blocks.cap: The three pyramids of Giza at the same scale, with the Statue of Liberty for size.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Giza sits on the desert edge west of the Nile. Find it near Cairo.

blocks.title: Biggest and smallest
blocks.q: Khufu's pyramid was about 147 m tall, Khafre's about 144 m and Menkaure's about 66 m. Which is the smallest, and by how much is it shorter than Khufu's?
steps: The smallest number is 66 m: Menkaure's.
blocks.a: Menkaure's, about 81 m shorter.

blocks.html: Thinking the Sphinx is far out in the desert. It is right at Giza, beside the causeway (a stone road) up to Khafre's pyramid. Many experts think its face shows Khafre, though no writing from his time says so.
How did people with no machines build the pyramids of Giza? Archaeologists have found many answers, and a few puzzles are still open.
Teams of skilled Egyptian workers cut stone with copper tools, dragged blocks on wooden sledges and raised them on ramps. Just how the ramps ran is still unknown.

Most of the stone was cut right at Giza. Fine white stone for the outside came by boat from Tura, across the river, and granite came from Aswan, far to the south. A papyrus diary kept by an official named Merer, found in 2013, records his team carrying stone by boat for Khufu's pyramid. Near the pyramids, archaeologists found the workers' town, with bakeries and the workers' own tombs.

blocks.name: eg-pyramid
blocks.cap: Build the pyramid layer by layer with the slider.

blocks.title: Moving a block
blocks.q: A team must move a heavy block across sand. What did Egyptians do?
steps: They put the block on a wooden sledge.
Workers pulled the sledge with ropes.
A tomb painting shows a worker pouring water on the sand in front of a sledge: wet sand is firmer, so the sledge slides more easily.
blocks.a: They dragged it on a sledge over wet sand.

blocks.title: Known or unknown?
blocks.q: Do we know exactly how the ramps were laid out: straight, zigzag or wrapped around the pyramid?
steps: Remains of ramps have been found at quarries and building sites.
But no ramp survives at the Great Pyramid, and experts suggest different plans.
blocks.a: No. That part is still unknown.

blocks.html: Thinking slaves built the pyramids, or that someone other than the Egyptians did. Archaeologists reject both ideas because of the evidence: the workers' town, their bakeries, their tombs, and their team names written on the stones.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Great Pyramid of Giza" (construction, the Diary of Merer and the workforce)

blocks.html: Ancient Egyptians lived by a river that flooded, under a sun that blazed every day. They believed the world was full of powers, and they gave those powers names. Here is what Egyptians believed about their gods.
The Egyptians believed in many gods, each caring for part of the world: Ra for the sun, Hapi for the flood, Nut for the sky, Geb for the earth, and Bes and Taweret for homes and families.

Each god explained something people saw or needed. The sun rose every morning: Egyptians said Ra sailed across the sky in a boat. The flood came every summer: they gave thanks to Hapi. Big temples were the gods' houses, where priests cared for a god's statue every day. At home, families kept small figures of household gods like Bes for protection.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: netjer, "god." The first sign is a flag on a pole, like the flags that stood in front of temples.

blocks.title: Which god?
blocks.q: Egyptians said one god sailed across the sky each day in a boat. Who was it?
steps: Sailing across the sky each day is what the sun does.
The sun god was Ra.
blocks.a: Ra, the sun god.

blocks.html: Thinking the gods were only animals. Egyptians pictured many gods as people, as animals, or as people with animal heads. The picture showed what a god was like, not a creature walking around. More on that in Gods with Animal Heads.
More than a thousand gods are known by name. Some were worshipped all over Egypt; others belonged to one town.
In Many Gods you saw that Egyptians pictured gods in different ways. Many gods have the head of an animal. Once you know the animals, you can name a god in any painting.
Tell gods apart by their heads: Horus the falcon, Anubis the jackal, Thoth the ibis, Bastet the cat, Hathor the cow (or cow horns), and Sobek the crocodile.

The animal was a clue to what the god did. A falcon flies high and sees far, like Horus, god of the sky and of kings. Jackals wandered near graveyards at the edge of the desert, so the jackal Anubis became the guardian of the dead. The ibis, a wading bird with a long curved beak, belonged to wise Thoth, god of writing.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The names of Horus (a falcon), Thoth (an ibis on a stand) and Anubis (ending with a lying jackal).

blocks.title: Name the god
blocks.q: A painting shows a god with a man's body and the head of a bird with a long, thin, curved beak. Who is it?
steps: A long curved beak belongs to the ibis.
The ibis-headed god is Thoth.
blocks.a: Thoth.

blocks.html: Mixing up Anubis and Bastet, or Horus and Thoth. Anubis is a jackal, with a long snout and tall pointed ears; Bastet is a cat. Horus has a falcon's short hooked beak; Thoth has an ibis's long curved beak.

sources.name: Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (1927), Sign-list G5 (falcon), G26 (ibis on a standard), E15 (jackal)

blocks.html: Egyptians told many stories about their gods. The most important was the story of Osiris and Isis. Different writers told it in different ways; here is its outline.

In the story, Osiris was a good king. His jealous brother Seth killed him. His wife Isis searched for him and, with her magic, brought him back. Osiris became ruler of the land of the dead, and their son Horus grew up to win back the throne.

The story explained things that mattered to every Egyptian. It said that death is not the end: Osiris lived again, so others hoped to as well. It said that a son should care for his father, as Horus did. And it explained the king: each living king was linked with Horus, and each king who died was linked with Osiris.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: Both names start with the throne sign, a seat. Isis often wore that sign on her head.

blocks.title: Who's who?
blocks.q: Which god in the story is the evil brother, and which is the son who wins the throne?
steps: Seth killed his brother Osiris.
Horus, son of Osiris and Isis, became king.
blocks.a: Seth is the brother; Horus is the son.

blocks.html: Thinking Osiris was the god of evil because he rules the dead. To Egyptians he was a kind king who gave new life. Paintings show him with green skin, the color of growing plants.
The oldest pieces of this story are in Egyptian tomb writings. A Greek writer, Plutarch, later told a long version with extra parts.

Egyptians believed in a life after death, and their gods, like Osiris, had shown the way. They believed the body was still needed in that next life. So families took great care of the bodies of people they loved.
Egyptians dried and wrapped the bodies of the dead so they would last. This is called mummification, and a body kept this way is a mummy.

In the dry desert, sand alone can dry a body and keep it for a long time. Egyptians learned to do this carefully. Skilled workers called embalmers covered the body in natron, a natural salt that soaks up water. Then they wrapped it in many layers of linen bandages, tucking in small lucky charms called amulets. The whole careful work took about 70 days.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs

opts.en: a mummy: the sign for mummies and statues

blocks.cap: The hieroglyph of a wrapped mummy.

blocks.title: In order
blocks.q: Put the main steps in order: wrap in linen; place in a coffin; dry with natron.
steps: First the body must be dried, so it will last.
Then it is wrapped in linen bandages.
Last, it is laid in a coffin.
blocks.a: Dry with natron, wrap in linen, place in a coffin.

blocks.title: Why natron?
blocks.q: Why did embalmers use natron, a kind of salt?
steps: Salt pulls water out of things (that is how salted fish keeps).
A dry body does not spoil.
blocks.a: To dry the body so it would last.

blocks.html: Thinking mummies are monsters from movies. A mummy is a real person whose body was kept with love by their family. Today scientists can look inside mummies with scanners, without unwrapping them.
Egyptians also mummified animals, such as cats and ibis birds, as gifts for the gods.
After a mummy was ready, it was laid in a tomb. Egyptians believed the dead would need things in the next life, much as they did in this one.
Tombs held grave goods: food and drink, furniture, clothes, jewelry, games, and little helper figures called shabtis that would do work for the dead person in the afterlife.

Egyptians imagined the next life as a better version of life by the Nile, with fields to farm and meals to enjoy. So they packed what a person would need. Shabtis held tiny hoes and baskets: if the dead person was called to work in the fields, the shabti would answer and do it instead. Families also brought fresh offerings of food to the tomb.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: hetep, "offering." The main sign shows a loaf of bread on a reed mat.

blocks.title: Why pack a game?
blocks.q: Tutankhamun's tomb held board games. Why would anyone put a game in a tomb?
steps: Egyptians believed the next life was like this one.
People enjoy games in this life.
blocks.a: So the dead person could enjoy playing in the afterlife too.

blocks.html: Thinking only kings had tombs. Many families had tombs too, from simple graves in the sand with a few pots, to painted rooms cut into the rock. Rich or poor, families gave their dead what they could.
Some tombs had several hundred shabtis, sometimes one for every day of the year, with overseer figures to keep them working.
The story of Osiris told Egyptians that the dead could live again. But they believed there was a test first, held before Osiris himself.

Egyptians believed a dead person's heart was weighed on a scale against the feather of Maat, which stood for truth and right. If the scale balanced, the person had lived a good life and could go on to the afterlife.

To Egyptians the heart was where your thoughts and your deeds were kept, so it remembered everything you had done. Wrongdoing made it heavy. A good, honest life kept it as light as the feather. The test taught that how you treat others matters. In paintings, the jackal god Anubis checks the scale, and Thoth, the ibis, writes down the result.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The words for heart and for Maat.

blocks.title: Who does what?
blocks.q: In a painting of the weighing, one god with a jackal's head works the scale, and one with an ibis's head holds a pen. Who are they?
steps: Jackal head: Anubis.
Ibis head, with a pen: Thoth, god of writing.
blocks.a: Anubis checks the scale; Thoth records the result.

blocks.html: Thinking the heart had to be heavy to pass. The heart had to balance the feather: as light as the feather, free of wrongdoing. Egyptians wrote spells for the test in the Book of the Dead, and the dead person declared, "I have not stolen, I have not lied."
Beside the scale waited a creature called Ammit, part crocodile, part lion and part hippopotamus. Egyptians hoped never to meet her!
Pyramids and temples were built for kings and gods. But where did ordinary families live? Their homes were much simpler, and they were made from the ground beside the Nile.
Most families lived in houses of mud brick, with a flat roof where people could work, store things and sleep on hot nights.

Mud from the river was free and everywhere. Mixed with straw and dried in the sun, it made strong bricks. Thick mud-brick walls kept houses cool by day. Windows were small and set high up, to keep out the hot sun. Stone was hard to cut and carry, so it was saved for things meant to last forever: temples, the gods' houses, and tombs.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: per, "house." The sign is a house seen from above, with a doorway in its wall.

blocks.title: Why so cool?
blocks.q: It is very hot outside. Why might a mud-brick house with small high windows feel cooler?
steps: Thick mud walls take a long time to heat up.
Small windows high in the wall let in little direct sunlight.
blocks.a: The thick walls and small windows keep out the heat.

blocks.html: Thinking people lived in stone buildings like temples. Stone was for gods and tombs; houses were mud brick. That is also why few ancient houses survive: mud brick crumbles, while stone lasts.
At Deir el-Medina, the village of the workers who cut the royal tombs, archaeologists found whole streets of houses. Most had four or five rooms, a kitchen at the back and stairs up to the roof.
In a mud-brick home, the kitchen was often at the back, open to the sky so smoke could escape. What was cooking? Mostly bread.
Everyday food was bread and thick beer made from grain, with onions, garlic, beans and lentils, fish from the river, and fruit like dates and figs. Meat was mostly for feast days.

Food came from what grew best by the Nile. Wheat and barley grew in the black mud, so bread and beer were eaten every day; beer was thick, almost like a soup, and gave energy. Cattle took a lot of land and food to raise, so beef was a treat for the rich or for festivals. Honey made food sweet; there was no sugar.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs

opts.en: a loaf of bread · a beer jug

blocks.cap: Two hieroglyphs from the kitchen: a loaf of bread and a beer jug.

blocks.title: Paid in bread
blocks.q: Workers who built the pyramids were paid partly in bread and beer. Why would that be useful pay?
steps: There were no coins yet.
Everyone needed bread and beer every day.
blocks.a: It was food that everyone needed, and there was no money yet.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians ate like kings every day. Most people ate simple bread and vegetables. Bread often had bits of sand and grit from grinding the grain, and scientists can see how it wore down the teeth of mummies.
Life in a mud-brick house beside the desert was hot. Egyptian clothes were made to keep people cool.
People wore light, white clothes of linen. Many wore wigs, and both men and women lined their eyes with dark eye paint.

Linen is made from the flax plant. It is thin and lets air through, perfect for hot days. Men usually wore a wrapped kilt, and women a long, close-fitting dress. Many people kept their hair very short or shaved and wore wigs on special days. Eye paint, called kohl, was made from crushed minerals; it may also have helped shade the eyes from the sun's glare.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: nebu, "gold." The sign is a broad collar of beads, the kind of necklace Egyptians loved to wear.

blocks.title: From plant to dress
blocks.q: Put in order: weave the linen cloth; grow the flax; sew a dress.
steps: First the flax plant must grow.
Its fibers are spun into thread and woven into linen.
Then the cloth is made into clothes.
blocks.a: Grow the flax, weave the linen, sew a dress.

blocks.html: Thinking only women wore eye paint. Men and women both did, and so did children sometimes. Look at almost any Egyptian painting: the dark lines around the eyes are on everyone.
Little children often wore nothing at all in the heat. Rich people wore jewelry: bead collars, bracelets and earrings.
Children in a mud-brick village had chores, but they also had time to play. Archaeologists have found their toys!
Children played with balls, dolls, spinning tops and toy animals. Families played board games such as senet, a game of 30 squares in three rows of ten.

Toys and games last when they are made of wood, clay or stone and buried in the dry sand. Some were put in tombs so their owners could play in the afterlife. Senet was a race: players threw sticks to see how far to move and tried to get all their pieces off the board first. Over time, Egyptians also linked the game with the journey of the dead.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs

opts.en: a game board with its pieces

blocks.cap: This hieroglyph shows a senet board seen from the side, with pieces on top. Scribes used it for the sounds mn.

blocks.title: Squares on the board
blocks.q: A senet board has 3 rows with 10 squares in each row. How many squares is that?
steps: Each row has 10 squares.
There are 3 rows: 3 × 10 = 30.
blocks.a: 30 squares.

blocks.html: Thinking ancient kids had no toys. Archaeologists have found balls of leather, wooden toy animals with jaws that open and shut, dolls, and spinning tops. Tomb paintings show people juggling, wrestling and playing ball games.
Another game, mehen, was played on a round board shaped like a coiled snake.
Bread for every meal meant someone had to grow the grain, grind it and bake it. Egypt needed many kinds of workers.
Most people were farmers. Others were bakers, brewers, potters, weavers, carpenters, builders, painters, fishermen, soldiers, priests and scribes.

Food came first: without farmers, nobody ate. Because farmers grew more grain than their families needed, the extra could feed people with other jobs. Skilled craftspeople worked in workshops for temples and the king. Sons often learned the same job as their fathers, and daughters learned to run a household, weave and bake.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs

opts.en: a sickle · a bull · a fish · a plant

blocks.cap: Hieroglyphs from the working world: a sickle, a bull, a fish and a plant.

blocks.title: Who makes it?
blocks.q: Who made the clay jars for storing grain and beer?
steps: Clay jars are shaped from wet clay, often on a turning wheel.
Then they are baked hard in a hot oven called a kiln.
That is the work of a potter.
blocks.a: A potter.

blocks.title: Why so many farmers?
blocks.q: Why did most Egyptians have to be farmers?
steps: Every person in Egypt needed food every day.
Farming was slow work done by hand, with simple tools.
It took many hands to grow enough grain for everyone.
blocks.a: Growing enough food for everyone took most of the people.

blocks.html: Thinking everyone in Egypt was a pharaoh or a slave. There were slaves, but most people were farmers and craftspeople. The tomb builders of Deir el-Medina were skilled workers who were paid in grain and other goods.
Egyptians wrote with beautiful picture signs called hieroglyphs. But writing was a special skill. The people who learned it were called scribes, and they kept Egypt running.
Scribes learned to read and write at school. They wrote with a thin reed pen, black and red ink, and sheets of papyrus, a paper made from a river plant.

A big kingdom needs records: how much grain each farm grew, how many workers came to work, what the taxes were, what the king ordered. Scribes wrote all of it down. Learning took years, so boys (and a few girls) started young, copying signs again and again on flakes of stone and broken pottery, which were cheaper than papyrus.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs

opts.en: a papyrus roll, tied and sealed

blocks.cap: A rolled-up papyrus, tied with string. This sign went at the end of words about writing.

blocks.title: Black and red
blocks.q: A scribe's palette held two cakes of ink, black and red. What was the red ink for?
steps: Black, made from soot, was used for most of the writing.
Red, made from a red earth called ochre, made some words stand out.
blocks.a: For headings and important words, so they stood out.

blocks.html: Thinking everyone could read. Only a small share of Egyptians, mostly scribes, could read and write. An old Egyptian school text tells students that a scribe's life is better than any other job, so they should study hard!
The papyrus plant grew in the marshes. Its stems were cut into thin strips, laid in two layers crosswise, pressed and dried into sheets.
Now that you know what scribes did, let's read like one. The first secret of hieroglyphs: many signs are not pictures of the word at all. They stand for sounds, like the letters of our alphabet.
Many hieroglyphs are sound signs. The owl 𓅓 is m, the water 𓈖 is n, and the mouth 𓂋 is r.

Pictures alone can't write everything. How would you draw "name" or "good"? Egyptians used pictures of things whose names began with a sound, and used them for that sound. So the mouth sign writes r even in words that have nothing to do with mouths. Egyptians wrote only the consonants, not the vowels.

head: Sign
Shows
Sound
blocks.cap: Ten easy sound signs.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: Mouth (r) and water (n) spell rn, said "ren," the word for "name."

blocks.title: Read a word
blocks.q: A word is written with a mouth and then water. What sounds does it spell?
steps: Mouth = r.
Water = n.
Together: r, n. Egyptologists say it "ren."
blocks.a: rn, "ren," which means "name."

blocks.html: Thinking every hieroglyph is a picture of the word. The owl in a word usually just means the sound m, not an owl! Ask: is this sign standing for a sound?

sources.name: Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (1927), Sign-list: the one-consonant signs (G17, N35, D21, X1, D58, I9, Q3, D46, S29, V31)

blocks.html: You can read sound signs. Hieroglyphs have two more kinds of signs that work with ideas, not sounds. Once you spot them, words become much easier to read.

Some signs are word signs: they mean just what they show, like the house sign for "house," often with a little stroke under it. Other signs are hint signs at the end of a word: they show what kind of thing the word is about, like walking legs for "go." Hint signs are not said out loud.

Egyptians did not write vowels, so many words looked alike. A hint sign at the end solved that. A seated woman says "this word is about a woman," the sun says "about time or light," and walking legs say "about moving." Experts call hint signs determinatives.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: zat, "daughter": a duck (sa), a loaf (t), and a seated woman as the hint sign.

blocks.name: eg-signsort
blocks.cap: Sort the signs: sound signs in one group, hint signs in the other. Then press Check.

blocks.title: Which hint sign?
blocks.q: A word ends with walking legs. What kind of word is it probably?
steps: Walking legs are a hint sign.
They show movement.
blocks.a: A word about moving, like "go" or "come."

blocks.title: Say it or not?
blocks.q: The word for "daughter" is written duck, loaf, seated woman. Which sign is not said?
steps: The duck is sa and the loaf is t: sat.
The seated woman is the hint sign.
blocks.a: The seated woman. The word is said "sat."

blocks.html: Trying to say every sign. Hint signs at the end of a word are silent; they only help you guess the meaning. Check: does the last sign show a kind of thing (person, sun, legs, water)? It is probably a hint sign.

sources.name: Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (1927), Sign-list A1, B1, D54, N5 (determinatives)

blocks.html: When you read sound signs, where do you start? English always goes left to right. Hieroglyphs can go left to right, right to left, or down in columns. Luckily, the signs themselves tell you.
People and animals face the start of the line. If the birds face left, start reading at the left. If they face right, start at the right. In a column, read from the top down.

Think of a parade walking toward you: you meet the leader first. Hieroglyph birds and people are like that parade, all facing the beginning. Egyptians chose the direction to fit the place: on a doorway, signs on the two sides could face each other, toward the door. Most often, they wrote from right to left.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The owl and the people face right, so this is read from right to left. Follow the arrow.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The same word facing left: now read from left to right.

blocks.title: Where to start?
blocks.q: In a line of hieroglyphs, the owl and the quail chick face to the right. Which end do you start at?
steps: Signs face the start of the line.
They face right, so the start is on the right.
blocks.a: Start at the right end.

blocks.html: Always starting on the left, as in English. Look at which way the birds face first, and start from that side. In a column, start at the top, and still check which way the signs face to know which column comes first.
With sound signs you can spell your own name. Egyptians spelled foreign names this way too, especially in later times, when Greek and Roman rulers had names that Egyptian had no words for.
Write your name with sound signs, one sign for each sound you hear: the owl for m, the water for n, the bread loaf for t.

Egyptian sound signs were not exactly our alphabet. There were no signs for our vowels, so for fun we borrow signs: the vulture for a, the reed for e or i, the lasso for o, the quail chick for u. When scribes wrote Greek names, they used the lion for l. A double letter, like the two n's in Anna, makes one sound, so it gets one sign.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: Type your name to see it in sound signs. This is a modern game, not how Egyptians wrote: their own names used fewer vowel signs.

blocks.title: Spell SAM
blocks.q: Which signs spell the name Sam?
steps: S: the folded cloth 𓋴.
A: the vulture 𓄿.
M: the owl 𓅓.
blocks.a: 𓋴𓄿𓅓 (cloth, vulture, owl).

blocks.html: Writing one sign for every letter, even silent ones. Write the sounds you hear. Kate ends in a silent e, so you might write k, a, t. And remember that Egyptians left out most vowels: in real Egyptian, a name would look shorter.
When you wrote Write Your Name, you put it inside an oval. That oval has a name: a cartouche. In real Egyptian writing, only special names got one.
A cartouche is an oval loop of rope drawn around a king's or queen's name. When you see one, you know you are looking at a royal name.

The loop is a rope tied at one end, like a ring that goes all the way around. Egyptians believed it surrounded and protected the name. French soldiers in Egypt around 1800 thought the oval looked like the paper cartridge for their guns, called a cartouche in French, and the name stuck. A king had several names, and the two most important were written in cartouches.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: Khufu, builder of the Great Pyramid: a round sign (kh), quail chick (u), viper (f), quail chick (u).

blocks.title: Read Khufu's cartouche
blocks.q: The cartouche holds: a round sign (kh), a quail chick (w), a horned viper (f), a quail chick (w). What name is it?
steps: Read the sounds in order: kh, w, f, w.
Between consonants, w is said "u": kh-u-f-u.
blocks.a: Khufu.

blocks.html: Thinking every word in a loop is a king's name. Cartouches hold only royal names. A long word or a word inside a box is something else.
Kings first wrote their names in cartouches near the start of the pyramid age, about 4,600 years ago.

sources.name: Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (1927), Sign-list V10 (cartouche)

blocks.html: Scribes counted grain, cattle and workers all day, so they needed numbers. Egyptian numbers are easy to read once you know six signs.
A stroke 𓏤 is 1, a hobble 𓎆 is 10, a coil of rope 𓍢 is 100, and a lotus 𓆼 is 1,000. Repeat a sign to add it up.

Egyptian numbers work by adding, not by place. Three strokes are 3. Two hobbles are 20. To read a number, count each kind of sign, multiply by its value, and add. Bigger numbers used a finger for 10,000, a tadpole for 100,000, and a kneeling god with raised arms for 1,000,000.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The number 1,325: one lotus, three coils, two hobbles, five strokes.

blocks.title: Read a number
blocks.q: Three coils of rope and two hobbles. What number is it?
steps: 2 hobbles × 10 = 20.

blocks.title: Write a number
blocks.q: How would you write 42?
steps: 42 = 4 tens + 2 ones.
So: 4 hobbles and 2 strokes.
blocks.a: Four hobbles and two strokes.

blocks.html: Reading the signs by place, like our digits. Egyptian numbers just add up: three coils and two hobbles is 320, in any order. There is no sign for zero, and none is needed.

sources.name: Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (1927), Sign-list Z1, V20, V1, M12, D50, I8 and C11 (the numerals)

blocks.html: For about 1,400 years, nobody could read hieroglyphs. The last ones were carved in AD 394, and then the knowledge was lost. You have learned to read cartouches; this stone is how people first learned to read them again.
The Rosetta Stone has the same message written three times: in hieroglyphs at the top, in Demotic (a fast everyday Egyptian script) in the middle, and in Greek at the bottom.

In 196 BC, Egyptian priests made a decree honoring King Ptolemy V and had it carved in three scripts, so that priests, ordinary Egyptians and the Greek-speaking rulers could all read it. In 1799, French soldiers found the stone near the town of Rosetta. Scholars could still read Greek. So they knew what the hieroglyphs had to say, and could start matching them up.

blocks.name: eg-scripts
blocks.cap: One decree, three scripts. The top is broken, so only 14 lines of hieroglyphs survive.

blocks.title: A key to the code
blocks.q: Why was the Greek part so important?
steps: The three parts say the same thing.
Scholars could read Greek.
So the Greek told them what the hieroglyphs meant.
blocks.a: It let scholars know what the hieroglyphs said, so they could work out the signs.

blocks.html: Thinking the stone is a dictionary. It is one priestly decree from 196 BC, copied in three scripts. It gave clues, not a word list. It took scholars more than twenty years to crack the code.
The stone has been in the British Museum in London since 1802. See it on the Timeline, with the other big moments of Egyptian history.
The Rosetta Stone was a puzzle. Many scholars tried to solve it. In 1822, a young Frenchman named Jean-François Champollion did.
In 1822, Champollion showed how hieroglyphs work: many signs stand for sounds, mixed with word signs and hint signs. He began with royal names in cartouches and used the Coptic language.

Names were the best place to start, because a name sounds about the same in every language. The Greek text named Ptolemy, so the cartouche must spell Ptolemy. Another cartouche, from an obelisk, spelled Cleopatra. The two names share sounds (p, t, o, l), and the same signs showed up in the right places! Champollion also knew Coptic, the last stage of the Egyptian language, so he could recognize Egyptian words once he sounded them out.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: Build Ptolemy's name from sound signs, the way Champollion read it: p, t, o, l, m, y, s.

blocks.title: A shared sign
blocks.q: The lion appears in both Ptolemy and Cleopatra. Which sound does it stand for?
steps: Ptolemy: p-t-o-l-m-y-s. Cleopatra: k-l-e-o-p-a-t-r-a.
The sound both names share in that spot is l.
blocks.a: The lion 𓃭 stands for l.

blocks.html: Thinking one person read the stone in a day. It took many scholars many years. The English scientist Thomas Young made early steps: he saw that cartouches held royal names and read some of the signs. Champollion cracked the system.
The story goes that when Champollion finally knew he was right, he ran to his brother shouting, "I've got it!" and fainted from excitement.
You met Tutankhamun, the Boy King, the boy king. For more than 3,000 years, his tomb lay hidden. Then, in 1922, an English archaeologist named Howard Carter found it.
In 1922, Howard Carter found the steps to Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings. It was nearly untouched and full of treasures.

Carter had searched the Valley for years, paid for by an English lord, Lord Carnarvon. On 4 November 1922, his team uncovered a step cut into the rock, then a staircase, then a sealed door. Peering in by candlelight, Carter was asked if he could see anything. "Yes, wonderful things," he answered. The tomb held golden shrines, furniture, chariots, jewelry and the famous gold mask.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The Valley of the Kings lies behind the cliffs on the west bank at Thebes (modern Luxor).

blocks.title: Why so slow?
blocks.q: The tomb held more than five thousand objects. It took Carter's team about ten years to empty it. Why so long?
steps: Every object had to be photographed and drawn exactly where it lay.
Fragile things had to be made safe before they could be moved.
blocks.a: Because they carefully recorded and protected every object before moving it.

blocks.html: Believing in a "curse" on the tomb. When Lord Carnarvon died of an infection in 1923, newspapers made up the curse story. But most of the people who entered the tomb lived long lives; Carter himself lived until 1939. There was no curse.
Howard Carter's slow, careful work at Tutankhamun's tomb shows what archaeology is really about. Archaeologists are detectives of the past.
Archaeologists dig carefully, write down exactly where everything was found, and study it to learn how people lived.

Where a thing is found is a clue, just like at a detective's crime scene. A pot found in a kitchen tells us about cooking; the same pot in a tomb tells us about burial customs. Once an object is lifted out, that clue is gone unless someone wrote it down. That is why archaeologists measure, photograph and draw before they move anything. Deeper layers of earth are usually older.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Egypt is full of places archaeologists study. Tap a dot to see what was found there.

blocks.title: A broken pot
blocks.q: You find a broken pot in a layer of ash under a house floor. What should you do first?
steps: Do not pull it out yet.
Photograph it, measure where it is and write it down.
Then lift it out carefully and label the bag.
blocks.a: Record exactly where it is before you move it.

blocks.html: Thinking archaeologists hunt for treasure. A plain potsherd or a seed can teach more than gold. They care most about where things were found and what they tell us about people's lives.

Today, many digs in Egypt are led by Egyptian archaeologists, and Egypt's laws say that ancient objects found there belong to Egypt. Scientists can even look inside mummies with scanners, without unwrapping them.
